Electrolytes and AKI in the surgical patient

brief.scenario: Mrs Susan Whitlock, 64, has 2 days of colicky central abdominal pain, repeated bilious vomiting and distension. She has not opened her bowels or passed wind for 24 hours. She had an open appendicectomy as a child and an abdominal hysterectomy at 45. Pulse 108, BP 112/70, temperature 37.4°C.
brief.task: The examiner will ask you about your assessment and management, giving results as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Probable adhesional obstruction. Resuscitate, decompress, and decide early whether the bowel is at risk.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Starting 'drip and suck' without looking for strangulation or a hernia.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "ABCDE, IV access, bloods with a lactate, then a fluid bolus."

grid.label: Resuscitation
grid.pass: ABCDE; IV access; bloods including lactate, U&E, FBC, CRP, group and save; 500 ml crystalloid bolus over under 15 minutes, then reassess.
grid.high: Catheter and hourly urine output; fluid balance chart; replaces nasogastric losses on top of maintenance.

grid.label: Examination for strangulation and hernia
grid.fail: Doesn't examine the hernial orifices or look for peritonism.
grid.pass: Examines the hernial orifices and scars; looks for peritonism, fever, tachycardia and a raised lactate.
grid.high: Knows examination misses about half of strangulations, so a normal abdomen doesn't exclude ischaemia.

grid.label: Decompression and electrolytes
grid.fail: Leaves her eating, or without a nasogastric tube while vomiting.
grid.pass: Nil by mouth; wide-bore nasogastric tube on free drainage; corrects electrolytes, especially potassium.
grid.high: Explains the tube reduces aspiration risk; checks renal function because dehydration causes AKI.

grid.label: Imaging
grid.fail: Relies on a plain abdominal X-ray to decide on surgery.
grid.pass: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to confirm obstruction, the transition point and any signs of strangulation.
grid.high: Names the signs needing surgery without delay: closed loop, ischaemia, free fluid.

grid.label: Water-soluble contrast challenge
grid.fail: Hasn't heard of the contrast challenge.
grid.borderline: Knows about the challenge but not the 24-hour film or what it shows.
grid.pass: Gastrografin orally or via the nasogastric tube; abdominal X-ray at 24 hours; contrast in the colon predicts resolution.
grid.high: Gives the dose (50–150 ml), and knows it is diagnostic and may also help the obstruction resolve.

grid.label: Indications for surgery (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Continues non-operative management despite peritonism or a rising lactate.
grid.pass: Surgery now for peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia; a non-operative trial is safe for up to 72 hours, so reviews for surgery if unresolved by then.
grid.high: Laparoscopy only in selected cases; plans consent for resection and possible stoma.

grid.label: Senior involvement and risk
grid.fail: Admits her without informing the registrar.
grid.pass: Registrar and consultant informed; risk of death documented by ST3 or above within 4 hours of admission.
grid.high: If predicted mortality is 5% or more: consultant surgeon and anaesthetist in theatre and critical care afterwards.

fail.text: How would you manage Mrs Whitlock?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you manage Mrs Whitlock?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ABCDE. IV access, bloods including a lactate, U&E, FBC, CRP, group and save. A 500 ml crystalloid bolus over less than 15 minutes, then reassess.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd examine her scars and hernial orifices, and look for peritonism.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Nil by mouth, a nasogastric tube on free drainage, and I'd correct her electrolytes, especially potassium.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast to confirm obstruction, find the transition point and look for strangulation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: It shows adhesional obstruction without ischaemia. Then?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Gastrografin down the tube and an abdominal X-ray at 24 hours. If contrast reaches the colon, it's likely to settle.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia, or if it hasn't resolved after 72 hours.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd tell my registrar and consultant, and her risk of death needs documenting within 4 hours by ST3 or above.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you manage Mrs Whitlock?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She's dehydrated and tachycardic. ABCDE, access, bloods with lactate, U&E, FBC, CRP, group and save. 500 ml Hartmann's over under 15 minutes, reassess. Catheter, hourly urine, and I'd replace her nasogastric losses on top of maintenance.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Two previous operations make adhesions likely, but I'd check her groins and scars for a hernia. Examination misses about half of strangulations, so a soft abdomen doesn't reassure me.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Nil by mouth and a wide-bore nasogastric tube on free drainage, mainly to stop her aspirating. Replace potassium, and watch her creatinine.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: CT abdomen and pelvis. I'm looking for a closed loop, poorly enhancing bowel or free fluid; any of those means theatre without delay.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: It shows adhesional obstruction without ischaemia. Then?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A water-soluble contrast challenge: 50 to 150 ml of Gastrografin via the tube, and an abdominal X-ray at 24 hours. Contrast in the colon predicts resolution; it may also help it resolve.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Now if she develops peritonism, fever or a rising lactate. Otherwise, if it hasn't resolved by 72 hours. Laparoscopy only if she's suitable; I'd consent for resection and a possible stoma.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Registrar and consultant now. Risk documented within 4 hours; if it's 5% or more, consultant surgeon and anaesthetist in theatre and a critical care bed.

failures.move: Continuing drip and suck in a patient with peritonism and a rising lactate.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: strangulated bowel becomes gangrenous or perforates.

failures.move: Not examining the groins in bowel obstruction.
failures.consequence: Misses an incarcerated hernia that needs surgery, not a contrast challenge.

failures.move: Using a plain abdominal X-ray to decide whether to operate.
failures.consequence: It doesn't show strangulation; CT does.

recovery.line: I'd also examine her groins and scars; a hernia changes the plan.

recovery.when: You can't remember the Gastrografin dose
recovery.line: I'd follow the local protocol for the dose; the key is an abdominal film at 24 hours.

knowledge.fact: Non-operative management first unless peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia: nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolytes.
Contrast in the colon on the 24-hour film predicts resolution. Non-operative trial is safe for up to 72 hours.
No resolution after 72 hours of non-operative management: surgery is recommended.
Gastrografin 50–150 ml orally or by nasogastric tube.
CT with IV contrast shows reduced bowel wall enhancement in ischaemia.
Predicted mortality of 5% or more is high risk.
Oral water-soluble contrast can be given with the CT or afterwards as the contrast challenge; take a 24-hour film either way.

recall.say: "Resuscitate, decompress, CT, and theatre if there's any sign of ischaemia."
do: NG tube, nil by mouth, potassium
recall.trap: A soft abdomen does not exclude strangulation.
recall.finish: Adhesiolysis, with resection if non-viable, when it fails or strangulates.

sources.name: ten Broek RPG, Krielen P, Di Saverio S, et al. Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO): 2017 update of the evidence-based guidelines from the World Society of Emergency Surgery ASBO working group. World J Emerg Surg 2018;13:24
sources.supports: Non-operative management first unless peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia; nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV fluids and electrolytes (low potassium common); examination detects strangulation in only 48%; bloods incl. lactate, electrolytes, renal function; plain films of limited value; CT with oral water-soluble contrast preferred; closed loop, ischaemia and free fluid mean surgery without delay; abdominal X-ray 24 h after contrast: contrast in the colon predicts resolution; non-operative trial safe for 72 h; laparoscopy for selected cases

sources.name: Di Saverio S, Coccolini F, Galati M, et al. Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO): 2013 update. World J Emerg Surg 2013;8:42
sources.supports: Gastrografin 50-150 ml orally or via nasogastric tube, at admission or after 48 h of conservative treatment; after 72 h of non-operative management without resolution, surgery is recommended

sources.name: NICE CG174: Intravenous fluid therapy in adults in hospital
sources.supports: Resuscitation: crystalloid containing sodium 130-154 mmol/l, bolus of 500 ml over less than 15 minutes (1.3.1)

sources.name: RCS England: The High-Risk General Surgical Patient: Raising the Standard
sources.supports: Standard 3: risk of death assessed and recorded by a senior surgeon (ST3 and above) within four hours of admission; standard 4: high risk = predicted hospital mortality 5% or more, and no recorded risk means treat as high risk; standard 8: consultant surgeon and consultant anaesthetist present, and immediate postoperative critical care admission

media.task: Describe the CT and say whether she needs theatre
media.description: Coronal CT abdomen with IV contrast showing dilated small bowel loops with a transition point and collapsed distal bowel, no closed loop

media.task: Say whether the contrast challenge predicts resolution
media.description: Abdominal X-ray 24 hours after Gastrografin showing contrast in the colon

partner.opening: Mrs Whitlock has just been referred to you from ED. How would you assess and manage her?

reveals.trigger: Asks for bloods and a gas
reveals.finding: Lactate 1.8 mmol/L, K 3.2, Na 134, urea 11.8, creatinine 118 (baseline 70), WCC 12.4, CRP 48.
Distended, tympanic, mildly tender centrally, no guarding. Midline and gridiron scars. Hernial orifices clear. Tinkling bowel sounds.
Dilated small bowel with a transition point in the pelvis and collapsed distal bowel. No closed loop, normal enhancement, no free fluid.

push.question: What on CT would make you operate now?
push.expect: Closed loop, reduced wall enhancement or ischaemia, free fluid.

push.question: How long would you continue non-operative management?
push.expect: Up to 72 hours if she has no signs of strangulation.

push.question: What standard applies to her risk assessment?
push.expect: Documented by ST3 or above within 4 hours; high risk if 5% or more.

curveballs.prompt: On day 2 she spikes 38.5°C, is tachycardic and guarding, lactate 3.9.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Signs of strangulation: stop non-operative management, resuscitate and take her to theatre with the consultant.

curveballs.prompt: She has a tender irreducible lump below the groin crease.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Likely obstructed femoral hernia: this needs surgery, not a contrast challenge.

curveballs.prompt: She has never had an operation.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Adhesions are less likely: CT to look for another cause, such as a hernia or tumour.
